topics.title: Start
topics.teach: Read the route. The pre-check is the official assessment on your program page.

topics.title: Texture
topics.teach: Sand is the largest of the three. Silt is in the middle. Clay is the smallest. A human hair is about sand, a spider web about silt, and cornstarch about clay.

topics.title: Ribbon
topics.teach: A ribbon longer than 2 inches is clayey. From 1 to 2 inches is clay loam. A lump that holds its shape but makes no ribbon is silty loam. A lump that falls apart is sandy.

fields.label: What a longer ribbon tells you about clay

topics.title: Water
topics.teach: Slower than 0.2 inches in an hour is clayey. From 0.2 to 6 inches in an hour is silty. Faster than 6 inches in an hour is sandy. Wetland kalo grows best where water stays.

fields.name: prediction
fields.label: A long sticky ribbon means water moves

fields.name: wetland
fields.label: Which texture wetland kalo needs, and what the water does

topics.title: Slope
topics.teach: Up to 8 percent is slight. From 8 percent through 15 percent is moderate. More than 15 percent is extreme.

fields.name: extreme
fields.label: What an extreme slope does, or how a terrace changes it

fields.name: flat
fields.label: What to do when water ponds on flat land

topics.title: Life
topics.teach: White fuzzy threads are the fungus group. A small animal with jointed legs is the insect group. A soft body making a tunnel is the worm group.

items.label: A soft body making a tunnel

fields.label: One job a named soil organism does for plants

topics.title: Land
topics.teach: For most plants, silty soil holds a useful amount of water. Sandy soil usually needs clay or other organic material. Clay soil usually needs larger particles so water can move.

topics.teach: A mahiʻai checks soil texture, slope, and soil organisms before choosing the crop and the water.
